subject: chemistry
title: Metallic bonding and properties of metals
key_idea: Metals are giant structures of positive metal ions in a regular pattern, surrounded by delocalised electrons. The attraction between the ions and the electrons is strong. This explains why metals have high melting points, conduct electricity and heat, and can be bent and shaped.

blocks.text: This section covers the structure of a metal and the bond that holds it together.

items.meaning: Outer-shell electrons from the metal atoms that are free to move through the whole structure.
The strong attraction between the positive metal ions and the delocalised electrons.

items: Metals have giant structures of atoms arranged in a regular pattern, in layers.
The outer-shell electrons of metal atoms are delocalised, so they are free to move through the whole structure.
This leaves positive metal ions surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons.
The sharing of delocalised electrons gives strong **metallic bonds**.
Most metals are shiny solids with high melting points and high density.
Metals are good conductors of electricity.
Most non-metals have low boiling points and are poor conductors of electricity.
A metal is a regular arrangement of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons.
The attraction between the ions and the electrons is a strong metallic bond.

blocks.text: The strong metallic bonds explain two properties: high melting and boiling points, and the ability to be bent and shaped.

items.text: Metals have giant structures with strong metallic bonding.
There are strong forces of attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons.
A lot of energy is needed to overcome these forces, so most metals have high melting and boiling points.

items: Malleable means a metal can be hammered or pressed into shape without breaking or cracking.
In a pure metal the layers of atoms (ions) can slide over each other.
The delocalised electrons keep the layers bonded as they slide, so the metal bends and does not break.

blocks.text: Pure metals are often too soft for many uses. They are mixed with other metals to make alloys, which are harder (see the note on alloys).

items: High melting point: strong forces between ions and electrons need a lot of energy to overcome.
Malleable: layers of ions slide over each other.

blocks.text: Metals are good conductors because the delocalised electrons are free to move.

items: **Electricity:** the delocalised electrons carry electrical charge through the metal.
**Thermal energy:** energy is transferred by the delocalised electrons.
Metals conduct in the solid and liquid state, because the electrons can move in both.

diagram.alt: Put the steps explaining how a metal conducts electricity in order.
diagram.prompt: Put the steps in order to explain how a metal conducts electricity.
steps: Metal atoms have outer-shell electrons that are delocalised.
The delocalised electrons are free to move through the structure.
A voltage is applied across the metal.
The electrons move through the metal and carry charge, so the metal conducts.

items: Metals conduct electricity because delocalised electrons carry charge through the metal.
Metals conduct heat because delocalised electrons transfer energy.
Electrons move, not ions.

checks.q: Describe the structure and bonding in a metal.
checks.a: Positive metal ions in a regular arrangement, surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons. There are strong forces of attraction between the ions and the electrons.

checks.q: Explain why metals have high melting points.
checks.a: There are strong forces of attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons. A lot of energy is needed to overcome them.
The layers of metal ions can slide over each other.

exam_phrases: (the electrons move) through the metal / structure
(delocalised electrons) move through the structure and transfer energy
layers of atoms can slide (pure metal)
different sized atoms distort the layers / structure
the movement of (delocalised) electrons is restricted

mistakes.wrong: Metals conduct electricity because they carry electricity or a current.
mistakes.right: Current and electricity are ignored. Say the (delocalised) electrons carry electrical charge through the metal.

mistakes.wrong: Metals conduct electricity because the ions move.
mistakes.right: It is the electrons that move and carry the charge. The positive metal ions stay in their layers.

mistakes.wrong: Copper conducts thermal energy because it has free particles.
mistakes.right: Name the particles. Say delocalised electrons move through the structure and transfer energy.

worked_example.question:
Aluminium is a metal.

Describe how metals conduct electricity.

Answer in terms of electrons.
answer_points: The electrons move through the metal (structure).
worked_example.tip: Current and electricity are ignored for charge, so write that the electrons carry charge.

exam_phrases: metal ions / cations surrounded by (delocalised) electrons
strong forces of attraction / bonding between (delocalised) electrons and metal ions
needs lots of energy to separate the particles / break bonds / break forces of attraction

mistakes.wrong: Metals conduct electricity because ions can move.
mistakes.right: Ions are rejected. Say electrons are delocalised, or can move.

mistakes.wrong: Metals have high melting points because of strong intermolecular forces between molecules.
mistakes.right: Mentioning intermolecular forces, covalent bonding, molecules, ionic bonding or atoms limits the answer to 1 mark. Say metal ions and delocalised electrons, with strong forces of attraction between them.

mistakes.wrong: Metals conduct because they have free electrons.
mistakes.right: 'Free' alone is ignored. Say the electrons can move, or are delocalised.

worked_example.question:
Metals have high melting points.

Explain, in terms of their structure and bonding, why metals have high melting points.
answer_points: Metal ions (cations) are surrounded by (delocalised) electrons.
There are strong forces of attraction (bonding) between the delocalised electrons and the metal ions.
A lot of energy is needed to separate the particles, break the bonds or break the forces of attraction.
worked_example.tip: Any two points score. Avoid intermolecular forces, covalent bonding and molecules.

exam_phrases: ions surrounded by a sea of electrons
strong forces of attraction between ions and electrons
has electrons that can move (through the metal)
layers / metal ions slide over each other

mistakes.wrong: Metals conduct electricity because they have free ions.
mistakes.right: Free ions score 0. Say electrons that can move through the metal, or delocalised electrons.

mistakes.wrong: Metals are malleable because the metal atoms or electrons slide over each other.
mistakes.right: Metal atoms and electrons are ignored. Say the layers (metal ions) slide over each other.

mistakes.wrong: A metal has covalent bonds between its atoms.
mistakes.right: Any reference to ionic or covalent bonding or intermolecular forces scores 0. Describe positive metal ions, a sea of electrons and strong forces of attraction.

worked_example.question: Describe the structure and bonding in a metal.
answer_points: The ions are surrounded by a sea of electrons.
There are strong forces of attraction between the ions and the electrons.
worked_example.tip: Name the particles (positive ions and electrons), then describe the attraction between them. Do not mention ionic or covalent bonding.
